notes.meaning: Jude introduces himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James. He writes to Christians who are called by God, held safe in His love, and kept secure in Christ. Rather than bragging about being Jesus' earthly relative, Jude chooses the humble title of bondservant.

Jude asks God to pour out mercy, peace, and love on his readers in overflowing amounts. Because dangerous deceivers were threatening the church, believers needed God's kindness and deep inner peace more than ever. These gifts reflect the goodness of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Jude had planned to write a peaceful letter about the salvation all Christians share. Instead, an urgent crisis forced him to plead with them to stand firm and defend the true faith. God handed down the gospel once for all time to His holy people, and its core message can never be altered.

Sneaky opponents had slipped into the church without being noticed. These ungodly teachers abused God's free grace by treating it as an excuse to live immoral lives, and in doing so they rejected Jesus as their only Lord. God's ancient warnings made it clear that men who act like this are headed for judgment.

differ.view: God in His sovereign and eternal decree marked out these ungodly men for condemnation before time began.
God did not decide their doom by an arbitrary decree, but foretold in ancient Scripture that anyone who willfully rebels will incur condemnation.

notes.meaning: Jude reminds his readers of the exodus from Egypt, a history they already knew well. Even though the Lord rescued the people of Israel from slavery, He later destroyed those among them who refused to believe. Starting out in God's blessings does not protect someone if they turn away in stubborn unbelief.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Several of the oldest Greek manuscripts read 'Jesus' instead of 'the Lord,' pointing to the eternal Son at work delivering and then judging Israel in the wilderness.

notes.meaning: God also judged the angels who refused to stay within the boundaries and authority He gave them. The Lord has locked these fallen spirits in dark, eternal chains until the great day of final judgment. Their punishment shows that no creature is too high or noble to escape God's justice.

The ancient cities of Sodom and Gomorrah plunged into gross sexual sin and unnatural desires. God destroyed them completely with fire, leaving them behind as an unmistakable warning for all generations. Their ruin illustrates the eternal punishment that awaits unrepentant sinners.

In the same foolish way, these false teachers follow their own dreams and pollute their physical bodies with sin. They despise God's rightful authority over their lives and insult glorious beings. Their inward fantasies lead directly to outward rebellion against God's order.

Even the mighty archangel Michael did not dare to trade insults with the devil when they argued over Moses' body. Instead of using abusive language, Michael simply said, 'The Lord rebuke you!' If a leading angel showed such restraint, proud men should never speak evil so carelessly.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Jude drew this account from Jewish tradition or the ancient work called the Assumption of Moses, citing the historical truth without making that non-biblical book part of Scripture.

notes.meaning: These arrogant men mock and slander spiritual truths that they do not even understand. The only things they do understand are their raw animal appetites, and by following those blindly, they destroy themselves. They act like beasts without reason rather than people created in God's image.

Jude pronounces a severe woe on these men because they walk in the footsteps of famous rebels from Scripture. Like Cain, they are driven by jealousy and hatred; like Balaam, they rush into sin just to make money; and like Korah, they rebel against God's authority and perish.

These men are like dangerous hidden reefs that can shipwreck the fellowship meals where early Christians ate together and celebrated the Lord's Supper. They feast without any fear of God and care only about indulging themselves. They are as empty as waterless clouds blown by the wind, and as dead as uprooted trees.

Jude compares these teachers to wild sea waves that churn up dirty foam, displaying their own shameful conduct for all to see. They are like wandering stars that offer no steady guide to travelers. Because of their deceptive path, God has reserved the deepest darkness for them forever.

Enoch, who lived before the great flood, prophesied that the Lord would return with tens of thousands of holy angels to judge the earth. God will convict all the ungodly for their wicked deeds and for the harsh, arrogant words they spoke against Him. God has always warned that rebellion will meet a sure and final end.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Jude quoted words preserved in the Jewish Book of Enoch under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, affirming the truth of the prophecy without declaring that entire apocryphal book inspired.

notes.meaning: These teachers are constant grumblers who complain about their lot in life while chasing their own selfish lusts. They boast with loud words to puff themselves up. At the same time, they flatter wealthy or powerful people just to get personal advantages.

Jude urges his readers to recall what the apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ foretold. The apostles warned that in the last times mockers would appear who make fun of the truth and chase their own ungodly passions. Remembering these warnings keeps believers from being shocked or deceived when trouble arises.

These men create divisions within the church, setting themselves up as spiritually elite while looking down on others. In reality, they are driven by purely natural desires and completely lack the Holy Spirit. A person who causes strife among God's people shows that they do not truly know God.

Instead of being led astray, Christians must build their lives on the firm foundation of true gospel doctrine. They are commanded to pray in the Holy Spirit, allowing God's Spirit to guide their thoughts, desires, and petitions. Real spiritual growth happens when faithful teaching and Spirit-led prayer work together.

Believers are told to keep themselves securely inside God's love. They do this by staying obedient and looking forward in hope to the return of Jesus Christ, who will bring them eternal life by His mercy. Walking closely with God is the believer's safe place while waiting for the Lord.

differ.view: True believers are kept safe by God's sovereign power and will never lose their salvation; keeping oneself is the fruit of that preservation, not a way to earn it.
Believers must actively watch and guard themselves in God's love, because anyone who presumes on past grace and turns to sin is in real danger of falling away.

notes.meaning: Jude directs the church to help wandering souls in different ways according to their condition. Those who waver in doubt need patient mercy and gentle guidance to bring them back. Others who are in deep danger must be snatched quickly from the fire of judgment, while believers stay watchful so they are not contaminated by the sins they seek to rescue others from.

Jude closes his letter with a radiant song of praise to the only wise God our Savior through Jesus Christ. God has the almighty power to guard His people from stumbling into ruin and to present them blameless and overflowing with joy before His glory. To Him belong all honor, majesty, rule, and authority before all time, right now, and for all eternity.
